extracted.intended_audience: administrative law commenters and practitioners (public interest advocates, attorneys, regulated parties) who submit comments or litigate agency procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and checklist for how commenters should monitor and engage across the variety of agency policymaking forms (notice-and-comment rulemaking, guidance, interpretive rules, adjudication, policy statements) and when to preserve or litigate objections to an agency's choice of procedural form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the commenter monitor and engage all relevant agency policymaking channels (not only formal NPRMs)?
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete commenter strategy includes monitoring and engaging across all these channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magill lists channels beyond formal notice-and-comment rulemaking: guidance documents (some solicit comments), interpretive rules, policy statements, formal and informal adjudications (which may establish precedent), petitions for rulemaking, comments on guidance documents, interpretive rule announcements, and informal staff statements. Practical guidance: set up monitoring for all these channels, respond when agencies solicit input, and use petitions for rulemaking when appropriate. Anti-pattern: waiting only for an NPRM and ignoring guidance or adjudicative developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where guidance functions as a substantive rule, does the comment object to the form choice?
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency uses guidance to do what should require notice-and-comment (a 'substantive rule' disguised as guidance), commenters can challenge the form itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identify and argue when guidance effectively acts as binding law. Key indicia listed: the guidance effectively binds regulated parties; it departs significantly from prior agency practice; it creates new substantive obligations. Practical steps: document how the guidance operates in practice, contrast it with prior practice, and explain why notice-and-comment was required. Anti-pattern: treating binding guidance as mere background and failing to press the form-choice objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the comment preserve form-choice objections for potential judicial review?
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should explicitly object when the agency's chosen form is procedurally inadequate, preserving the issue for judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve reviewable objections, a commenter must clearly state that the agency's chosen form (e.g., guidance rather than notice-and-comment) is procedurally inappropriate and request the appropriate form (e.g., rulemaking). Practical guidance: make a contemporaneous administrative record of the objection and request corrective procedure; use specific legal arguments (e.g., that the action constitutes a 'substantive rule') so courts can later entertain the claim. Anti-pattern: raising the form-choice argument only post hoc in litigation without having preserved it in the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the comment engage the legal weight of the form chosen (binding rule vs. interpretive guidance)?
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy form chosen affects both the participation channel and the legal weight of the comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and argue the legal consequences of the particular form: notice-and-comment rules are binding and require agencies to respond to substantive comments; guidance documents typically have weaker procedural protections and less legal force; interpretive rules and policy statements get more deferential judicial review; adjudications can create precedent and privilege parties to the proceeding. Practical guidance: tailor arguments to the form’s legal consequences (e.g., emphasize substantive harms and statutory notice requirements when the agency treats guidance as binding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the commenter consider filing a petition for rulemaking when guidance is being used inappropriately?
rubrics_metrics.description: When guidance is being used inappropriately, the commenter should consider a petition for rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petition for rulemaking is a direct administrative tool to push the agency to use notice-and-comment procedures instead of guidance. Use petitions when guidance imposes obligations that should be adopted through formal rulemaking or when the agency refuses to adopt required procedures. Practical tip: combine petitioning with public comments and, if necessary, preserve litigation options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use notice-and-comment to require agency response to substantive comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment requires response to substantive comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies must respond to significant comments in rulemaking, commenters should use notice-and-comment opportunities to force agencies to address substantive concerns on the record. Strategy: raise detailed, evidence-backed objections and alternatives so the agency must address them. Scoring note: a strong comment in notice-and-comment can alter agency decisions because of the mandatory response obligation. Anti-pattern: submitting vague or perfunctory comments that the agency can ignore without substantive reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: If policy is being made through adjudication, ensure participation and preserve the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudications privilege parties to the proceeding and may establish precedent for agency policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When agencies set policy via adjudication, affected parties should seek party status or otherwise participate to influence results and create a record. Practical steps: intervene or petition for participation where possible, raise procedural and substantive objections in the adjudicative record, and preserve arguments for appellate review. Anti-pattern: treating adjudicative outputs as isolated and failing to engage, despite their potential precedential effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that interpretive rules and policy statements receive deferential review and adjust strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive rules and policy statements receive deferential judicial review compared to substantive rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts often defer to agencies on interpretive rules and policy statements, commenters should calibrate expectations and legal strategies accordingly—e.g., focus on administrative record-building, statutory arguments, and clear evidence that a guidance document functions as a substantive rule requiring notice-and-comment. Practical guidance: emphasize statutory limits and practical effects of the guidance to overcome deference; otherwise consider procedural preservation for later challenge.
